instructions: See docs/ratings.md. Give every season a rating on the absolute scale. Rate the player that season, never their career.

seasons.note: Wenger's arrival turned a squad player into a first-choice one; the double season is where he becomes genuinely good.
Ten years on from the previous season here: a mature, England-capped midfielder rotating through the unbeaten Arsenal side.
Thirty-two and down to eleven starts at Middlesbrough; the last of him in the top flight.

A Netherlands, Ajax and Juventus goalkeeper playing for a promoted side: the club was mid-table, the goalkeeper was one of the two or three best in the division. Rated at the Lehmann/Seaman tier for distribution and command of the area.

Rated above his Fulham seasons deliberately: in his mid-thirties he was the most reliable goalkeeper in England, and the record clean-sheet run is evidence of handling and positioning, not of the defence alone.
A title and a European final in a farewell season; commanding as ever, and thirty-nine.
Thirty-seven and playing every week for a relegated Wolves side: still the most reliable defender there, but a long way from the United full-back in pace and level.
Three starts - Neil Sullivan took the Tottenham shirt. Rated as the keeper, not on the appearances.
Three seasons on from the last rated one, aged 37 and back from Sporting: still commanding and a fine shot-stopper, but nine points off the peak and no longer near the best in the world.
Twelve goals at 18 in his first season; already an exceptional finisher, not yet an exceptional footballer.
Twenty-five goals and PFA Young Player; the finishing was already the best in the country.
His peak: 28 league goals at 20, and as pure a finisher as English football produced in the decade. Below Shearer's 91 because the all-round game was narrower.
Cruciate ruptured in February; nineteen starts, and he never regained the movement.
Fifteen starts behind Owen and Heskey, but decisive in the cup treble; the finishing was still the best in the country when he played.
Hip and knee trouble and twelve starts at Manchester City. By 27 the sharpness of movement that made him had gone, and this is where it shows.
Thirty-six starts, seven goals, and Liverpool’s most reliable passer that season.
Outstanding from his first season in England; dominant aerially and calm on the ball, a little short of the very best centre-backs.
The defensive spine of the treble side and in the PFA Team of the Year; commanding in the air and a genuinely good passer.
Thirty-four and rotated out of the first choice pair; still reads the game as well as anyone at the club, but no longer covers the ground for it.
Ruptured a cruciate in April 1997 and managed only 14 starts; rated as the diminished player of that season.
Fully recovered at 34 and Coventry's best player, which earned the Liverpool move.
Thirty-five and the controlling influence on the treble run-in; a fine passer whose game never depended on legs.
Converted from a wide forward into a central one and became a different, better player.
The best season of his career: 18 league goals in a treble side, and among the most complete forwards in Europe that year.
Four starts and out of Ferguson’s plans by Christmas. The fall-off in condition and application was real, not just rotation.
Reinvented at Sunderland as a screening midfielder rather than a forward: useful, experienced, a long way below the United striker.
Nineteen and already a regular in a side that finished third; rated as the promising teenager he was, not the 400-game veteran he became.
The two Inter seasons are absent from the file; he returned to England at essentially the level he left it.
Thirty-five and captain of a relegated Wolves side; the engine that defined him has gone.
First full season as Blackburn’s first-choice left-back; England call-up followed.
The best left-back in the country that season, and a title winner.
Broke an ankle in December; thirteen starts, and he was not the same athlete for over a year.
Six starts through injury.
Twenty and unknown in England; transformed Arsenal’s midfield within weeks of arriving.
A double season and PFA Team of the Year: physically the most dominant midfielder in the league and technically its equal.
Captain of an unbeaten title side. Physically dominant and technically excellent — genuinely world class.
Thirty-three and used in short spells: the physical range that defined him has gone, and with it most of what made him a 90.
The long throw is the trait: at Stoke his delivery into the box was a genuine top-flight weapon, which nothing else about his game was.
A seven-point rise in one season at 19-20: pace and finishing that already looked elite, 17 league goals and PFA Young Player. Held below the Cole 1993/94 anchor (86) on all-round game.
A half-season loan at Liverpool after two indifferent years abroad; the pace and touch were intact, the goals were not.
Fourteen goals in an ever-present season for a mid-table City; a complete, mobile centre-forward well short of the very top.
Eighteen starts before leaving for Fenerbahçe in January.
Returned to Arsenal from Everton in February 1993.
His peak years: England's man-marker, and the better of the two first-choice Arsenal centre-backs by this point.
Thirty-six and beginning to be rotated; the pace that let him man-mark is going.
Aged 37 and a fringe option by the Invincibles season.
Twenty at the start of the Double season and first choice for it; the athleticism and the recovery pace were already exceptional, the defensive detail still coming.
The best left-back in the league at 22 and England’s first choice.
Moved to Villa in March 1995; the same player in both halves of the season.
Moved to Villa in March 1995; the same player in both halves of the season.
Thirty-seven, three starts in his final season and a bench option in a double-winning side.
PFA Player of the Year and his peak: 25 goals with the best leap in the division.
Persistent injuries from the Tottenham move onwards; never a first-choice-quality forward again.
Twelve goals from twenty starts in a relegated Leicester side at 36; the leap is still there and almost nothing else is.
Eight goals and eight assists in a debut Premier League season at 21; a genuinely good technician in a newly promoted side.
Every minute of every league game at nineteen; quick, tireless and already a better attacking outlet than most left-backs in the division.
A broken ankle in February ended his season and cost him the left-back place for good.
Record fee for a keeper in November 1993; 12 earlier starts for Southampton.
Injured and displaced by John Filan; rated on ability, not on the ten starts.
Joined Blackburn in March 1995 and started the run-in of the title season.
Joined Blackburn in March 1995 and started the run-in of the title season.
Fourteen assists and England's first-choice wide player; comfortably his best season.
Six starts. The hernia and hamstring problems that defined the rest of his career start here.
Joined Everton in November 1996.
Joined Everton in November 1996.
His best Everton season, which earned the move across Stanley Park.
Eighteen and already unhurried on the ball in a Premier League midfield; rated as the promising teenager, not the Manchester United player.
Nineteen and a first-choice Premier League midfielder; the range of passing was already the best thing about a poor West Ham side.
Nine goals in eight starts on arriving from Trabzonspor. A hot streak in a relegation fight, not a step change in ability, so the rating moves three points and not nine.
Eight starts at 33; the pace had gone and Everton had moved on to Rooney.
Twenty-three in his first English season and immediately Chelsea’s quickest and most athletic defender; capable at centre-back and either full-back without loss.
Mostly at left-back in a title-winning side that conceded fifteen; elite as a defender, and better still for being able to do it anywhere across the back four.
Thirty-seven starts in a side that finished fourth, mostly as a wide midfielder doing a full-back’s defensive job.
Two years on and a different player: an energetic, ball-winning central midfielder in a seventh-placed side, capped by England the following year.
An England cap at 22 and the engine of the Sunderland midfield in a seventh-placed side.
Seventeen for most of the season and already the division's joint top scorer. Rated for genuinely elite pace and finishing at the time, not for what he became.
Hamstring damage carried from the 1999 injury cost him a yard of the pace that defined him; fewer starts and a less decisive player.
Sixteen league goals and the two that won the FA Cup final; the hamstring trouble had been managed and the pace was back.
Ballon d’Or winner: nineteen league goals, the Munich hat-trick, and the most feared runner in Europe. Held just below Shearer (91) because the all-round centre-forward game was narrower.
Sixteen goals but visibly a fraction slower and increasingly dropping into midfield areas.
The hamstring and metatarsal years have taken the yard of pace the whole game was built on; still a fine finisher, no longer a runner.
Nineteen, thirty-four starts and eight league goals in a survival season; the timing of the runs into the box was the finished part of his game from the start.
Twelve league goals and the captaincy of a promoted side; the best season of his career, two years on from the last rated one.
Dropped for Carroll after the Porto error; the ability had not changed much but the season was a fragmented one.
Ever-present across four Everton seasons and at his best in the last two; a reliable, athletic top-half keeper rather than an elite one.
Signed from Cambridge and broke his leg in his third start; a capable but still unproven top-flight forward at this point.
Regular first-team football at Coventry finally showed what he was, three years after the broken leg at United.
Eighteen goals, a share of the Golden Boot and an England cap: his peak.
Joined Aston Villa in November 1998.
Joined Aston Villa in November 1998.
Back from the broken neck of December 1999 and a regular again, but no longer the runner he was.
Rated as the twenty-year-old breaking through in the double season, not the player of 1999.
Runner-up for the Ballon d’Or; the best right-sided midfielder in the world that season. Elite delivery and range of passing, ordinary one-v-one.
